topic: the Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference

easy.text: Which two outcomes are most associated with the late-19th-century 'Scramble for Africa'? (Select all that apply)

options.text: European powers rapidly carved up nearly the entire African continent into colonies
options.feedback: Correct -- by 1914, European powers controlled almost all of Africa.

options.text: African kingdoms were invited to help negotiate the new borders
options.feedback: No African representatives took part in the key negotiations that divided the continent.

options.text: Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained largely free of European colonial rule
options.feedback: Correct -- these two states were the rare exceptions that avoided formal European colonization.

options.text: Africa's precolonial kingdom borders were left completely unchanged
options.feedback: European powers redrew borders with little regard for existing African political or ethnic boundaries.

medium.text: Which two developments are most associated with the 1884-85 Berlin Conference that regulated the Scramble for Africa? (Select all that apply)

options.text: European powers agreed to rules for claiming African territory, such as demonstrating 'effective occupation'
options.feedback: Correct -- the conference set procedural ground rules for competing colonial claims.

options.text: No African leaders or representatives were invited to participate
options.feedback: Correct -- the conference decided Africa's fate without any African voices present.

options.text: The conference immediately granted independence to all African colonies
options.feedback: The opposite occurred -- the conference facilitated colonization, not independence.

options.text: The conference was hosted in Africa itself, in Cairo
options.feedback: The conference was hosted by German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck in Berlin, not in Africa.

hard.text: Which two of the following were among the very few African territories that avoided formal European colonization during the Scramble for Africa? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Ethiopia decisively defeated an invading Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, preserving its independence.
Correct -- Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, remained independent throughout the colonial era.
Egypt fell under British occupation and control starting in 1882.
Algeria was a French colony for over a century.
Nigeria was consolidated as a British colony during this era.

easy.easy: The two truths are nearly total continental partition by European powers, and the near-total exclusion of African voices from that process -- not African participation or unchanged borders.
easy.medium: One correct outcome is about how much territory changed hands; the other is about which countries managed to stay independent.
easy.hard: Think about how much of the map changed color on European colonial maps by 1914.

medium.easy: Both truths involve the conference's actual procedural content -- an occupation-based rule for claims and the complete absence of African attendees -- not any promise of independence or an African host city.
medium.medium: The correct answers involve who set the rules for claiming territory, and who was left out of the room.
medium.hard: This 1880s meeting set the ground rules European powers followed when claiming African land.

hard.easy: One of these two nations is in the Horn of Africa and famously defeated a European invader; the other was founded by freed American slaves.
hard.medium: Both correct nations avoided colonization for different reasons -- one through a decisive military victory, the other through its unusual founding history.
hard.hard: Rule out the two nations that were, in fact, colonized (one by Britain, one by France) -- the remaining two are the actual exceptions.

easy.text: The Boer Wars were fought primarily between the British Empire and settlers of which European descent in southern Africa?

options.text: Dutch descent (the Boers, later known as Afrikaners)
options.feedback: Correct -- 'Boer' means 'farmer' in Dutch, and referred to descendants of mostly Dutch settlers in southern Africa.
Portugal colonized Mozambique and Angola nearby, but the Boer republics were settled by people of Dutch descent.
Some French Huguenots settled early in the region, but the Boer identity and wars centered on Dutch-descended settlers.
Germany colonized German South-West Africa nearby, but the Boer republics were Dutch-descended, not German.

medium.text: What valuable resource discoveries in the Boer republics of Transvaal and the Orange Free State sharply increased British interest in the region before the Second Boer War?

options.feedback: Correct -- diamond discoveries at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand made the Boer republics enormously valuable to Britain.
Oil was not the resource at stake -- it was diamonds and gold.
Rubber wealth is more associated with colonial holdings in Africa's rainforests and Southeast Asia, not the Boer republics.
Silver was not the key resource -- gold and diamonds drew British interest to the Boer republics.

hard.text: What controversial British tactic during the Second Boer War (1899-1902), used against Boer guerrilla fighters and their families, drew international condemnation?

options.text: Concentration camps that held Boer civilians, where disease and malnutrition caused many deaths
options.feedback: Correct -- Britain interned Boer civilians in camps to undercut guerrilla support, and poor conditions led to widespread suffering.

options.text: Mass deportation of Boer civilians to India
options.feedback: Boer civilians were interned within southern Africa in camps, not deported overseas to India.

options.text: A naval blockade of Boer coastal cities
options.feedback: The Boer republics were landlocked interior states -- Britain's controversial tactic was on land, not a naval blockade.

options.text: Forced conscription of Boer men into the British army
options.feedback: Boer fighters resisted Britain as guerrillas -- they were not conscripted into the British army.

easy.easy: These settlers' name comes from the Dutch word for 'farmer.'
easy.medium: This group descended mainly from Dutch colonists who settled southern Africa centuries earlier.
easy.hard: This group is distinct from Portuguese, French, or German colonial populations elsewhere in southern Africa -- their name literally means 'farmer' in their own language.

medium.easy: Two specific valuable minerals, one used in jewelry and one a precious metal, were found in Boer territory.
medium.medium: Neither resource was oil, rubber, or silver -- think sparkling gemstones and a precious yellow metal.
medium.hard: One resource is famous from a South African city named for a British colonial administrator; the other is mined from a ridge whose name is now a global mining term.

hard.easy: This tactic involved rounding up civilians into guarded camps, not deportation, conscription, or a naval blockade.
hard.medium: This controversial practice is remembered today as an early, notorious use of civilian internment camps.
hard.hard: This method targeted the guerrillas' support base directly, by interning noncombatants rather than deporting, conscripting, or blockading them.

easy.text: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 restored political power in Japan to which figure, ending centuries of military rule?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Meiji Restoration returned real political authority to the emperor, ending the shogunate system.
The shogun headed the very military government system that the restoration ended.
The daimyo lost regional power under the new centralized imperial government, rather than gaining it.
Japan did not yet have a prime minister in this modern sense at the time of the restoration itself.

medium.text: Which system of military rule did the Meiji Restoration bring to an end in Japan?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Meiji Restoration ended over two centuries of rule by the Tokugawa shogunate.
The Qing dynasty ruled China, not Japan -- it was a separate ruling house entirely.
The Yuan dynasty ruled China centuries earlier, unrelated to Japan's Meiji-era shogunate.
The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea, not Japan.

hard.text: Which slogan captured the Meiji government's core strategy of rapid modernization and militarization to resist Western domination?

options.feedback: Correct -- this slogan captured the Meiji government's drive to modernize Japan's economy and military simultaneously.

options.text: Sonno joi ('Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians')
options.feedback: This was an earlier anti-foreign rallying cry used before the restoration, not the actual Meiji-era modernization policy.
Bushido refers to the traditional samurai code of conduct, not the government's modernization slogan.
Manifest Destiny was a 19th-century American expansionist idea, unrelated to Japan's modernization.

easy.easy: This figure had been a symbolic ruler for centuries before regaining real power in 1868.
easy.medium: This figure's restoration to real power gives the era its name.
easy.hard: This figure is distinct from the military ruler (shogun) and regional lords whose power the restoration ended.

medium.easy: This was the specific shogunate ruling Japan right up until 1868.
medium.medium: This ruling family's name is often used alongside 'shogunate' for Japan's last era of military rule before 1868.
medium.hard: This shogunate, not any Chinese or Korean dynasty, is what the Meiji Restoration abolished.

hard.easy: This phrase pairs national wealth with military might as twin goals.
hard.medium: This slogan is different from an earlier anti-foreigner rallying cry and from the samurai code of honor.
hard.hard: This is the actual modernization-era slogan, distinct from the pre-Restoration 'expel the barbarians' slogan, the samurai's ethical code, and an unrelated American expansionist idea.

easy.text: The Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) was fought between the Russian Empire and which rising Asian power?

options.feedback: Correct -- Japan fought and defeated Russia in this 1904-1905 conflict.
China was not the combatant against Russia in this war -- Japan was.
Korea was a contested territory in the region but not the power fighting Russia directly.
The Ottoman Empire was not involved in this conflict -- it was fought by Japan and Russia.

medium.text: The Russo-Japanese War is often noted as significant because it marked what kind of first in modern history?

options.text: The first modern military victory of an Asian power over a major European power
options.feedback: Correct -- Japan's victory stunned the world as the first time in the modern era an Asian nation defeated a major European power.

options.text: The first war to use airplanes
options.feedback: Airplanes were not yet used in warfare -- that came later, notably in World War I.

options.text: The first war ended by the United Nations
options.feedback: The United Nations did not exist yet in 1905 -- the war was ended by a treaty mediated by the U.S. president.

options.text: The first war fought entirely at sea
options.feedback: The war included major land battles, such as the siege of Port Arthur, not just naval combat.

hard.text: Which decisive naval battle in 1905, where Japan's fleet under Admiral Togo destroyed most of Russia's Baltic Fleet, effectively sealed Japan's victory?

options.feedback: Correct -- Japan's crushing naval victory at Tsushima effectively ended Russia's ability to continue the war at sea.
Midway was a World War II Pacific battle decades later, unrelated to the Russo-Japanese War.
Jutland was a World War I naval battle in the North Sea, not part of the Russo-Japanese War.
Trafalgar was a Napoleonic-era naval battle a century earlier, unrelated to Japan and Russia.

easy.easy: This nation, an island power in East Asia, stunned the world by defeating a much larger European empire.
easy.medium: This country had rapidly modernized just decades earlier and used its new military against Russia.
easy.hard: This is the same East Asian nation whose late-19th-century modernization is remembered by a name meaning roughly 'enlightened rule.'

medium.easy: This achievement was about which side of the East-West divide won, not about which branch of the military fought.
medium.medium: No airplanes and no United Nations existed yet -- think about who beat whom, for the first time in the modern era.
medium.hard: The 'first' here is geopolitical, not technological or institutional -- an Asian nation defeating a European empire, not a first in aviation or international arbitration.

hard.easy: This battle's name is not from World War II or World War I, but from a strait between Japan and Korea.
hard.medium: This naval clash effectively finished off Russia's fleet after a long voyage from the Baltic Sea.
hard.hard: This battle is distinct from Midway (Pacific, WWII), Jutland (North Sea, WWI), and Trafalgar (Napoleonic era) -- it's named for the strait where Russia's Baltic Fleet met its end.

easy.text: The completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869 connected the eastern United States to which region?

options.feedback: Correct -- the railroad linked the eastern rail network all the way to California.
Florida and the Gulf Coast were not the destination of this railroad -- it reached the Pacific coast.
This was a U.S. domestic railroad, not a link to Canada.
This was a U.S. domestic railroad, not a link to Mexico.

medium.text: The two railroad companies that built the transcontinental railroad, meeting in Utah in 1869, were the Union Pacific and which other company?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento to meet the Union Pacific building westward.
The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad was an earlier eastern U.S. railroad, not the one that met the Union Pacific in Utah.
The Southern Pacific developed later and separately -- the Central Pacific was the actual partner company in 1869.
The Canadian Pacific Railway was a later, separate Canadian project, not part of this U.S. railroad.

hard.text: Which group of immigrant laborers made up the majority of the workforce that built the Central Pacific Railroad's treacherous route through the Sierra Nevada?

options.feedback: Correct -- Chinese immigrant laborers performed the grueling and dangerous work of blasting through the Sierra Nevada for the Central Pacific.
Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans made up much of the Union Pacific's workforce building westward, while Chinese immigrant labor dominated the Central Pacific's route.
German immigrants were not the dominant workforce on this specific mountain route -- Chinese laborers were.
Italian immigrants were not the dominant workforce on the Central Pacific's Sierra Nevada route -- Chinese laborers were.

easy.easy: This is the Pacific coast state whose 1850 statehood followed a massive gold rush.
easy.medium: This region had recently become a state after a famous gold discovery.
easy.hard: This region is on the opposite coast from where the railroad started, tied together for the first time by rail.

medium.easy: This company built the western portion of the line, starting from Sacramento.
medium.medium: This company's name pairs with 'Pacific' but refers to the middle of the country, not the north or south specifically.
medium.hard: This is distinct from an earlier eastern railroad, a later southern route, and Canada's own national railway -- it's the company that laid track eastward from California.

hard.easy: This group crossed the Pacific Ocean to work on the railroad, distinct from the European immigrant groups who worked the other end of the line.
hard.medium: This workforce is often distinguished from the Irish immigrants and war veterans who built the Union Pacific's portion.
hard.hard: This group built through the hardest mountain terrain, the Sierra Nevada, while a different immigrant group dominated the flatter Union Pacific route.

easy.text: The California Gold Rush began after gold was discovered in 1848 at which site?

options.feedback: Correct -- gold was found at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, triggering the rush.
Ellis Island was a later immigration processing station in New York, unrelated to the gold discovery.
Fort Sumter is associated with the start of the Civil War, not the Gold Rush.
Plymouth Rock is associated with early Pilgrim settlement, centuries before the Gold Rush.

medium.text: Who is credited with discovering the gold at Sutter's Mill that triggered the California Gold Rush?

options.feedback: Correct -- Marshall, an employee building the mill, spotted the gold flakes that started the rush.
The mill was owned by John Sutter, but it was his employee James Marshall who actually found the gold.
Levi Strauss later became famous for making durable trousers for miners, but he did not discover the gold.
Brigham Young led Mormon settlers to Utah around the same era, unrelated to the gold discovery.

hard.text: The huge influx of prospectors during 1849, nicknamed the '49ers,' contributed directly to which major political milestone for California in 1850?

options.text: California's admission to the United States as a state
options.feedback: Correct -- the rapid population growth from the Gold Rush helped California achieve statehood in 1850.

options.text: California's independence as its own nation
options.feedback: California became a U.S. state, not an independent nation.

options.text: The founding of the Republic of Texas
options.feedback: The Republic of Texas was a separate, earlier and unrelated development.
Alaska's annexation happened later, in 1867, and is unrelated to California's Gold Rush-era statehood.

easy.easy: This site was a small mill in the foothills of California, owned by a Swiss immigrant.
easy.medium: This location's name is also linked to the mill owner, a man whose name became attached to a nearby fort as well.
easy.hard: This is the specific mill, not a famous immigration station, Civil War fort, or Pilgrim landing site.

medium.easy: This person was an employee working at the mill, not its owner.
medium.medium: This is not the man who owned the land, nor the jeans maker, nor the Mormon leader of the same era.
medium.hard: Distinguish the mill's owner from the man who actually spotted the gold while building it -- the discoverer is the answer, not the owner or other era figures.

hard.easy: This milestone made California an official part of the country, not an independent nation.
hard.medium: Rule out Texas and Alaska -- this is specifically about California's status changing in 1850.
hard.hard: This is a statehood milestone, distinct from Texas's earlier independence or Alaska's later, unrelated annexation.

topic: westward expansion and the Homestead Act

easy.text: Which two things characterized the Homestead Act of 1862, part of America's westward expansion? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It offered settlers a set amount of free public land (160 acres)
options.feedback: Correct -- the act offered 160-acre plots of public land to settlers.

options.text: It required settlers to live on and improve the land for several years to gain full ownership
options.feedback: Correct -- settlers had to reside on and improve the land, typically for five years, to receive title.

options.text: It was signed by President Thomas Jefferson
options.feedback: The Homestead Act was signed by President Abraham Lincoln in 1862, decades after Jefferson's presidency.

options.text: It only applied to land east of the Mississippi River
options.feedback: The act applied to western public lands, not land east of the Mississippi.

medium.text: Which two statements accurately describe the Homestead Act's role in westward expansion? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was signed into law by President Abraham Lincoln in 1862
options.feedback: Correct -- Lincoln signed the act during the Civil War.

options.text: It encouraged settlement of western territories by offering land nearly for free
options.feedback: Correct -- the near-free land was a major incentive for settlers to move west.

options.text: It guaranteed statehood to any territory within one year of settlement
options.feedback: The act had nothing to do with granting automatic or rapid statehood -- it was about individual land claims.

options.text: It primarily targeted land in New England
options.feedback: The act applied to western public lands, not New England, which was already long settled.

hard.text: Which two of the following are accurate about the broader consequences of the Homestead Act and westward expansion? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It contributed to a rapid increase in the number of farms and settlers across the Great Plains
options.feedback: Correct -- millions of acres were claimed and settled by farming families under the act.

options.text: It accelerated the displacement of Native American nations from their traditional lands
options.feedback: Correct -- the rapid influx of settlers put severe pressure on Native nations' lands and ways of life.

options.text: It was limited exclusively to U.S. Army veterans
options.feedback: The act was open broadly to qualifying settlers and citizens, not restricted only to veterans.

options.text: It required settlers to pay the full market price for their land upfront
options.feedback: The whole point of the act was to make land available for little to no upfront cost, in exchange for residency and improvement.

easy.easy: The two truths involve the specific acreage offered and the multi-year improvement requirement -- not the signing president or a false geographic restriction.
easy.medium: Think about the land amount and the residency requirement -- not who signed it or where it applied.
easy.hard: One correct fact is about how much land was offered for free; the other is about what settlers had to actually do to keep it.

medium.easy: Both truths concern the law's 1862 origin under a wartime president and its function as a land incentive -- not a statehood guarantee or an eastern U.S. focus.
medium.medium: This law made land nearly free to attract settlers -- it didn't guarantee automatic statehood or target New England.
medium.hard: One truth is about which president signed the law; the other is about why it drew settlers west.

hard.easy: The two truths describe rapid agricultural settlement growth and the displacement pressure this put on Native nations -- ruling out the false veteran-exclusivity and upfront-payment claims.
hard.medium: Both truths involve consequences for settlers moving in and for Native nations already there -- not veterans-only access or full upfront payment.
hard.hard: One truth is about population growth on the plains; the other is about the law's impact on people already living there.

easy.text: Which two things helped trigger the United States entering the Spanish-American War in 1898? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The mysterious sinking of the USS Maine in Havana harbor
options.feedback: Correct -- the explosion and sinking of the USS Maine inflamed American public opinion against Spain.

options.text: American public outrage and sensationalized 'yellow journalism' news coverage
options.feedback: Correct -- sensational newspaper coverage stirred public demand for war with Spain.
Germany was not involved in invading Cuba -- the conflict was between the U.S. and Spain.

options.text: A Spanish attack on Pearl Harbor
options.feedback: Pearl Harbor was attacked by Japan decades later, in 1941, unrelated to the Spanish-American War.

medium.text: Which two territories did Spain cede to the United States as a result of the Spanish-American War? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States under the 1898 Treaty of Paris.
Correct -- Puerto Rico was also ceded to the United States by Spain.

options.text: Cuba, as a formal U.S. territory
options.feedback: Cuba gained nominal independence rather than becoming a formal U.S. territory.
Hawaii was annexed by the United States through a separate process around the same era, not ceded by Spain.

hard.text: Which two outcomes specifically resulted from the 1898 Treaty of Paris that ended the Spanish-American War? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Spain relinquished its remaining major colonial claims in the Caribbean and Pacific
options.feedback: Correct -- the treaty marked the effective end of Spain's colonial empire in these regions.

options.text: The United States gained control of Guam
options.feedback: Correct -- Guam was among the Pacific territories transferred to the United States.
Mexico was not part of this treaty or conflict at all.

options.text: Spain retained full control of Cuba
options.feedback: Spain lost control of Cuba, which gained nominal independence rather than remaining under Spanish rule.

easy.easy: The two triggers are a specific ship's sinking and inflammatory press coverage -- ruling out unrelated wartime events from other conflicts entirely.
easy.medium: Think about a ship explosion and how newspapers stirred public anger -- not any German or Japanese involvement.
easy.hard: One trigger was a dramatic naval disaster in a Cuban harbor; the other was how the American press covered it.

medium.easy: Both correct territories were formally ceded by the defeated colonial power in the peace treaty -- distinct from Cuba's separate independence status and Hawaii's unrelated annexation.
medium.medium: Cuba got nominal independence rather than becoming a U.S. territory, and Hawaii's annexation was a separate process -- focus on the other two.
medium.hard: One territory is a Pacific island chain; the other is a Caribbean island, both ceded by the losing side.

hard.easy: The two true outcomes are Spain's broad colonial withdrawal and the specific transfer of one named Pacific island -- not any claim involving Mexico or continued Spanish rule over Cuba.
hard.medium: Rule out any mention of Mexico or continued Spanish control of Cuba -- neither happened.
hard.hard: One outcome is broad (Spain's colonial losses); the other is a specific small Pacific island.

easy.text: The Philippine-American War (1899-1902) broke out after the United States annexed the Philippines instead of granting it what?

options.feedback: Correct -- Filipino revolutionaries had expected independence, and fought when the U.S. annexed the islands instead.
Statehood was never the issue at stake -- Filipinos sought full independence, not U.S. statehood.
The conflict was about political sovereignty, not a trade arrangement.
The conflict was about political sovereignty, not a military alliance.

medium.text: Which Filipino revolutionary leader, who had earlier fought against Spain, led the resistance against U.S. rule in the Philippine-American War?

options.feedback: Correct -- Aguinaldo led Filipino forces first against Spain, and then against the United States.
Rizal was an inspirational nationalist writer executed by Spain in 1896, before this war, but he did not lead the military resistance against the U.S.
Ho Chi Minh led Vietnam's independence movement in a different country and era, unrelated to the Philippines.
Sun Yat-sen was a Chinese revolutionary leader, unrelated to the Philippine independence struggle.

hard.text: Compared to the Spanish-American War that preceded it, how does the Philippine-American War compare in terms of scale and cost?

options.text: It was longer and far deadlier, involving brutal guerrilla warfare and significant civilian suffering
options.feedback: Correct -- the Philippine-American War dragged on for years and caused far more casualties than the brief Spanish-American War.

options.text: It was much shorter and caused almost no casualties
options.feedback: The opposite is true -- this war was longer and much deadlier than the Spanish-American War.

options.text: It never actually involved any combat
options.feedback: The war involved extensive and brutal combat, including guerrilla warfare.

options.text: It was fought entirely by naval forces with no land battles
options.feedback: This was primarily a land-based guerrilla conflict, not a naval-only war.

easy.easy: This is the specific political status -- full self-rule -- that was expected but denied, sparking the new conflict.
easy.medium: This is the self-governing status many Filipinos expected once Spanish rule ended.
easy.hard: Filipino revolutionaries had expected this outcome after helping defeat Spain, but the U.S. had other plans.

medium.easy: This is the actual military and political leader of Filipino resistance in this specific war, distinct from an earlier martyred writer and from revolutionary leaders of other Asian nations.
medium.medium: This is not the executed writer-hero from the earlier anti-Spanish movement, nor a leader from Vietnam or China.
medium.hard: This leader had already led forces against Spanish colonial rule before turning against the new American administration.

hard.easy: This later conflict dragged on far longer and proved dramatically more costly in lives, driven by grinding guerrilla combat rather than quick, decisive battles.
hard.medium: This war involved extensive guerrilla fighting on land, not a brief bloodless standoff or a purely naval conflict.
hard.hard: Weigh how this conflict's duration and human toll compared to the shorter war against Spain that came right before it -- the difference is significant.

easy.text: The Mexican Revolution, beginning in 1910, was launched largely to overthrow which long-ruling Mexican leader?

options.feedback: Correct -- Diaz had ruled Mexico for decades, and the revolution sought to end his long authoritarian rule.
Zapata was a revolutionary leader fighting against the ruling regime, not the ruler being overthrown.
Santa Anna was a Mexican leader from decades earlier, in the 19th century, unrelated to the 1910 revolution.
Juarez was an earlier reformist president from the mid-19th century, not the ruler the 1910 revolution targeted.

medium.text: Which revolutionary leader is most associated with the rallying cry 'Tierra y Libertad' ('Land and Liberty') and land reform for Mexico's rural peasants?

options.feedback: Correct -- Zapata led peasant forces in southern Mexico under the banner of land reform for rural communities.
Villa was a major northern revolutionary general known for military campaigns, but this specific land-reform slogan is most linked to Zapata.
Diaz was the ousted dictator the revolutionaries fought against, not a champion of this peasant land-reform slogan.
Madero was the revolution's early leader and president, not the figure most associated with this specific peasant land-reform slogan.

hard.text: The Mexican Revolution ultimately led to the adoption of what major foundational document in 1917?

options.feedback: Correct -- the 1917 Mexican Constitution enshrined many revolutionary reforms and remains foundational today.
The Treaty of Versailles ended World War I in Europe, unrelated to Mexico's own revolution.
The Monroe Doctrine was an earlier U.S. foreign policy statement, not a Mexican document.
The Platt Amendment concerned U.S.-Cuba relations, unrelated to Mexico's revolution.

easy.easy: This leader had ruled Mexico for decades before revolutionaries rose against him.
easy.medium: This figure's long, authoritarian rule is what the revolution sought to end, not any of the revolutionary fighters themselves.
easy.hard: Distinguish the ousted ruler from the revolutionary generals fighting against him, and from earlier 19th-century Mexican leaders.

medium.easy: This leader operated mainly in southern Mexico and championed peasants' land rights.
medium.medium: This is not the northern general known for military raids, nor the ousted dictator, nor the revolution's first president.
medium.hard: This figure's specific slogan concerns land redistribution for peasants -- distinct from a northern military leader, the deposed dictator, or the revolution's earlier presidential figurehead.

hard.easy: This document reorganized Mexico's government and enshrined revolutionary reforms.
hard.medium: This is a purely Mexican domestic document, unrelated to a WWI peace treaty, U.S. foreign policy doctrine, or a Cuba-related amendment.
hard.hard: Rule out documents tied to World War I, U.S. hemispheric policy, or Cuban-American relations -- the actual answer is Mexico's own new founding legal document.

easy.text: During World War I, the Ottoman government carried out the systematic killing and forced deportation of members of which ethnic group, an event now widely recognized as genocide?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Ottoman government's WWI-era campaign against Armenians is known as the Armenian Genocide.
Some Ottoman Greeks also faced persecution in this era, but the event specifically named the Armenian Genocide targeted Armenians.
This specific, widely recognized genocide targeted Armenians, not Kurds.
Persians were not the group targeted by this Ottoman campaign -- Armenians were.

medium.text: Around what date in 1915 is the beginning of the Armenian Genocide traditionally marked, commemorated today as Armenian Remembrance Day?

options.feedback: Correct -- this date marks the arrest and execution of Armenian intellectual and community leaders in Constantinople, traditionally seen as the genocide's start.
October 29, 1914 is when the Ottoman Empire entered World War I -- months before the genocide's traditional start date of April 24, 1915.
May 24, 1915 is when the Allied Powers first publicly condemned the killings as 'crimes against humanity' -- about a month after the genocide's traditional start date.
July 28, 1914 marks the outbreak of World War I in Europe, not the start of the Armenian Genocide, which began the following year.

hard.text: Death marches during the Armenian Genocide forced deportees into which desert region, where many died from starvation, exposure, and violence?

options.feedback: Correct -- deportees were forced on death marches into the Syrian Desert, with Deir ez-Zor becoming a notorious endpoint.
The Negev Desert, in present-day Israel, was not the route of these death marches -- deportees were driven into the Syrian Desert.

options.text: The Nefud Desert in northern Arabia
options.feedback: The Nefud Desert lies further south on the Arabian Peninsula -- the death marches were directed into the Syrian Desert.

options.text: The Arabian Desert's Rub' al Khali
options.feedback: This deep Arabian desert region was not the deportation route -- the Syrian Desert was.

easy.easy: This is the specific group whose WWI-era persecution gives this genocide its name -- not other Ottoman minority groups.
easy.medium: This Christian ethnic minority's persecution during WWI is the event most specifically called by this name.
easy.hard: This group's homeland lay partly within the Ottoman Empire's eastern territories.

medium.easy: This date falls in the spring of 1915, marked annually in remembrance.
medium.medium: This date is specific to spring 1915, not the Ottoman Empire's entry into WWI the year before or the Allied condemnation issued a month later.
medium.hard: Distinguish this date from the Ottoman Empire's WWI entry in late 1914, the general outbreak of WWI in mid-1914, and the Allied 'crimes against humanity' declaration in May 1915.

hard.easy: This desert lies within Ottoman Syria itself, not in Palestine, Arabia's Nefud region, or the Arabian Peninsula's deep southern interior.
hard.medium: This region is associated with a specific Ottoman-era Syrian town that became a notorious deportation endpoint.
hard.hard: This is the Middle Eastern desert region tied to the deportation route's endpoint, distinct from the Negev, the Nefud, or the Arabian Peninsula's Empty Quarter.

easy.text: The Zimmermann Telegram was a secret message from Germany proposing a wartime alliance with which country against the United States?

options.feedback: Correct -- Germany proposed a military alliance with Mexico in the event the U.S. entered World War I.
Canada was a British ally in the war, not the country Germany tried to recruit against the U.S.
Cuba was not the target of Germany's proposed alliance -- Mexico was.
Brazil was not the target of Germany's proposed alliance -- Mexico was.

medium.text: What did Germany offer Mexico in the Zimmermann Telegram in exchange for joining the Central Powers against the U.S.?

options.text: Help reclaiming territory including Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona
options.feedback: Correct -- Germany dangled the return of formerly Mexican territory in the American Southwest.

options.text: Full annexation of the United States
options.feedback: Germany's offer was about specific southwestern territories, not the entire United States.
The Panama Canal was not part of Germany's offer to Mexico.

options.text: A permanent seat at a future League of Nations
options.feedback: The League of Nations did not yet exist and was not part of this 1917 offer.

hard.text: What was the most direct consequence of the Zimmermann Telegram's interception and publication in early 1917?

options.text: It significantly increased American public support for entering World War I against Germany
options.feedback: Correct -- public outrage over the telegram helped push American opinion toward joining the war.

options.text: It caused Mexico to immediately declare war on the United States
options.feedback: Mexico did not act on Germany's proposal or declare war on the U.S.

options.text: It led to the founding of the League of Nations
options.feedback: The League of Nations was founded years later after the war ended, not as a direct result of this telegram.

options.text: It caused the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
options.feedback: That assassination happened in 1914, years before this 1917 telegram, and triggered the war's start, not this event.

easy.easy: This is the specific North American nation Germany tried to recruit as an ally, not Canada, Cuba, or Brazil.
easy.medium: Germany hoped this southern neighbor of the U.S. would open a second front against America.
easy.hard: This country shares a long border with the United States.

medium.easy: The offer specifically dangled the return of formerly Mexican territory in the American Southwest -- not the Canal, a League seat, or full U.S. annexation.
medium.medium: This isn't about the Panama Canal or a future peace organization -- it's about specific U.S. states.
medium.hard: The offer involved land the U.S. had gained decades earlier, in its own southwest.

hard.easy: The real consequence is a shift in U.S. public sentiment toward entering the war, distinct from a Mexican declaration of war, the League's founding, or the war's original 1914 trigger.
hard.medium: Rule out a Mexican declaration of war, the League's founding, and the 1914 assassination -- the actual consequence played out in how people back home reacted, not on a foreign battlefield or at a later peace conference.
hard.hard: Consider what typically happens to a nation's mood at home when it learns of a hostile foreign plot aimed squarely at it, and match that general effect to one of the four options.

topic: the Russian Revolution and the Bolsheviks

easy.text: Which two events made up the Russian Revolution of 1917? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The February Revolution, which forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate
options.feedback: Correct -- the February Revolution ended tsarist rule in Russia.

options.text: The October Revolution, in which the Bolsheviks seized power
options.feedback: Correct -- the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, seized power later that same year.
The storming of the Bastille happened in France in 1789, unrelated to Russia's 1917 revolution.
The Cuban Revolution happened decades later, in the 20th century, unrelated to Russia's 1917 events.

medium.text: Which two statements accurately describe the events of 1917 in Russia? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A Provisional Government briefly replaced the deposed tsar
options.feedback: Correct -- a Provisional Government ruled Russia between the February and October revolutions.

options.text: The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, overthrew that Provisional Government later in the year
options.feedback: Correct -- Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government in the October Revolution.

options.text: Tsar Nicholas II remained in power throughout 1917
options.feedback: Nicholas II abdicated in February 1917 and did not remain in power.

options.text: The Bolsheviks were led by Leon Trotsky as their supreme leader
options.feedback: Trotsky was a major Bolshevik organizer, but Lenin was recognized as the movement's supreme leader.

hard.text: Which two developments directly followed the Bolsheviks' October Revolution seizure of power? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A prolonged Russian Civil War between Bolshevik 'Red' forces and anti-Bolshevik 'White' forces
options.feedback: Correct -- years of civil war followed the Bolshevik takeover.

options.text: The eventual formation of the Soviet Union
options.feedback: Correct -- the Bolshevik victory ultimately led to the founding of the USSR in 1922.

options.text: Russia's immediate entry into World War I on the side of the Allies
options.feedback: Russia actually exited World War I, signing a separate peace with Germany, rather than continuing to fight on the Allied side.

options.text: The restoration of the Romanov dynasty to the throne
options.feedback: The Romanov dynasty was not restored -- the Bolsheviks consolidated a new communist government instead.

easy.easy: The two 1917 events are the tsar's ouster and the later Bolshevik seizure of power -- ruling out revolutions from entirely different countries and centuries.
easy.medium: Both events happened in Russia in 1917 -- not France in 1789 or Cuba in the 20th century.
easy.hard: One event forced out the old monarchy; the other brought a new revolutionary party to power later the same year.

medium.easy: Both truths involve the sequence of a temporary post-tsarist government followed by Lenin's Bolsheviks toppling it -- not continued tsarist rule or Trotsky as supreme leader.
medium.medium: The tsar did not stay in power, and Trotsky, while a major figure, was not the top Bolshevik leader.
medium.hard: One truth is about a temporary government; the other is about who replaced it later that year.

hard.easy: The two real consequences are a multi-year civil war and the later founding of the USSR -- not continued participation in WWI or a monarchist restoration.
hard.medium: Russia actually left World War I rather than joining the Allies, and the old royal family was not restored.
hard.hard: One consequence was years of internal armed conflict; the other was a new communist state's eventual creation.

easy.text: The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was an early international organization created mainly to do what?

options.text: Prevent future wars through collective diplomacy and cooperation
options.feedback: Correct -- the League was founded to resolve disputes diplomatically and prevent another world war.
Trade tariff coordination was not the League's core mission -- preventing war was.
Currency management was not the League's core mission -- preventing war was.
Space exploration did not exist as a concern in 1920 -- the League's mission was preventing war.

medium.text: Although he championed its creation, which country never actually joined the League of Nations?

options.feedback: Correct -- despite President Wilson's advocacy, the U.S. Senate refused to ratify membership.
France was a founding member of the League, not the country that stayed out.
The United Kingdom was a founding member of the League, not the country that stayed out.
Japan was actually a founding member of the League, though it later withdrew in 1933 -- it is not the country that never joined at all.

hard.text: The League of Nations is widely considered to have ultimately failed at its core mission because it could not stop which kind of events in the 1930s?

options.text: Aggressive territorial expansion by member and non-member states, such as Japan's invasion of Manchuria and Italy's invasion of Ethiopia
options.feedback: Correct -- the League's failure to stop these invasions revealed its inability to enforce collective security.
The Great Depression was an economic crisis, not the kind of military aggression the League specifically failed to stop.

options.text: The rise of jazz music in the United States
options.feedback: This is an unrelated cultural development, not a matter of international security.

options.text: The completion of the Panama Canal
options.feedback: The Panama Canal was completed years earlier, in 1914, and is unrelated to the League's core failures.

easy.easy: This is about preventing armed conflict specifically, not managing trade, currency, or space exploration -- none of which existed as international concerns yet.
easy.medium: This body aimed to settle disputes diplomatically rather than through war.
easy.hard: This organization's founding purpose is right there in the idea of nations forming a 'league.'

medium.easy: This country's president had proposed the organization, yet its own Senate refused to ratify membership.
medium.medium: This is not one of the wartime Allied European powers, nor an Asian founding member that later withdrew -- it's the country whose own leader pushed hardest for the idea.
medium.hard: The irony here is that the nation whose president most championed this idea never actually joined -- distinct from European Allied powers or the founding Asian member that left later.

hard.easy: The core failure was an inability to stop military aggression and territorial conquest -- not the Depression, a music trend, or an unrelated engineering project.
hard.medium: Think of a Horn of Africa nation and an East Asian region both invaded in the 1930s despite the League's existence.
hard.hard: The failures involved countries invading and annexing other territories, not economic or cultural developments.

topic: the rise of fascism in Mussolini's Italy

easy.text: Which Italian leader founded the Fascist movement and became known as 'Il Duce' ('The Leader')?

options.feedback: Correct -- Mussolini founded Italian Fascism and ruled Italy as 'Il Duce.'
Hitler led Nazi Germany, a separate country and movement, though later allied with Mussolini's Italy.
Franco led Spain's Nationalist forces and later ruled Spain, not Italy.
The king appointed Mussolini as prime minister but was not the founder of the Fascist movement himself.

medium.text: What event in 1922 pressured Italy's king into appointing Mussolini as prime minister?

options.feedback: Correct -- this show of force by Fascist supporters marching on the capital pushed the king to appoint Mussolini.
The Beer Hall Putsch was Hitler's failed 1923 coup attempt in Germany, not this Italian event.
Kristallnacht was a 1938 Nazi pogrom in Germany, unrelated to Mussolini's 1922 rise.
Italy's invasion of Ethiopia came later, in 1935, well after Mussolini had already come to power.

hard.text: Mussolini's Fascist government pioneered a system of state-controlled economic organization, blending nationalism with tight government-business coordination, known as what?

options.feedback: Correct -- corporatism organized industry and labor under tight state direction in Fascist Italy.
Fascism explicitly rejected communism's class-struggle basis, positioning itself as an alternative to it.
Fascist Italy rejected hands-off, free-market economics in favor of tight state coordination.
Feudalism was a much older medieval land-based system, unrelated to Mussolini's modern economic model.

easy.easy: This leader's nickname translates simply as 'The Leader.'
easy.medium: This founder of Fascism ruled Italy before Hitler rose in Germany or Franco in Spain.
easy.hard: Distinguish Italy's fascist founder from Germany's Nazi leader, Spain's Nationalist general, and Italy's own king, who merely appointed him.

medium.easy: This event was a show of force -- supporters marching on Italy's capital city to demand power.
medium.medium: This is not a German or Spanish event, and it predates Italy's later invasion of an African nation.
medium.hard: This 1922 Italian event is distinct from Germany's failed 1923 coup attempt, Nazi Germany's 1938 anti-Jewish pogrom, and Italy's own later 1935 invasion.

hard.easy: This economic system tightly links business and the state under nationalist goals, unlike free markets or class-based revolution.
hard.medium: This isn't communism's class struggle or laissez-faire's hands-off approach, and it's not a medieval land-based system.
hard.hard: The correct term describes fascist Italy's own blend of nationalism and state-directed economic coordination -- distinct from communism, free-market capitalism, and feudalism.
